newsitem.title: USA: Widows of US Civil War veterans meet at Gettysburg.
newsitem.headline: Widows of US Civil War veterans meet at Gettysburg.

text.p: Their husbands fought on opposite sides in the U.S. Civil War in the last century, yet the frail war widows on Tuesday reached out to touch each other in an extraordinary display of unity and forgiveness.

The meeting on the 134th anniversary of the battle of Gettysburg united 96-year old Daisy Anderson, who married a former slave and Union soldier in 1927, with Alberta Martin, 90, who wed an ageing Confederate veteran in 1922.

The women, now confined to wheelchairs, are two of the last three surviving widows of fighters of the Civil War, which was fought between 1861 and 1865. They met in an old farmhouse used by Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee as his headquarters early in the battle of Gettysburg that began 134 years ago on Tuesday.

The three-day battle ended in a brutal defeat for Lee that helped turned the military tide against the South. The war divided the North and the secessionist South over slavery and states' rights. It was finally won by the North.
"I wanted to meet you so bad I didn't know what to do. I'd like to kiss you," Anderson said.
"You're one of a kind. I'm so glad to meet you," replied Martin, who was holding a bouquet of flowers and a small Confederate flag in her lap.
The two exchanged kisses on the cheek, warmly shook hands and chatted for about 10 minutes, reaching out several times to touch one another or hold hands.

Martin, who lives with her son in Elba, Alabama, gave Anderson a 19th century locket with a picture of Martin inside. Anderson, who moved into a Denver nursing home 3-1/2 years ago after a hard life of manual labour in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, expressed regret she was unable to organise a reciprocal gift.

Both women received commemorative medals from the organisations of Union and Confederate army descendants who organised the meeting, then went outside to watch as flags of the two warring sides were raised.

They were to ride in a fringed surrey to the centre of Gettysburg and join a funeral procession for a set of human remains found last year and believed to be those of a battle casualty. Both said they would think of their husbands at a burial ceremony in Gettysburg National Military Park, although neither of the men fought in that battle.
Asked why she had come to the event and to meet Martin, Anderson said, "It reminded me of my husband and I think it shows unity, and that's what we need."

Anderson's husband, Robert, fled slavery in Kentucky and joined the U.S. Coloured Troops in 1864. He remained in the Army after the Civil War and was sent West to fight Indians as an African American "buffalo soldier."
He died in a car accident eight years after marrying Daisy Anderson.
Martin's husband, William Jasper Martin, joined the Confederate Army in 1864. He was 81 when the two married, and the couple had one son, also named William.

Martin is recognised as the last surviving Confederate widow. The Sons of Union Veterans group has identified one Union widow besides Anderson, Bertha January, but have been unable to locate her or obtain more information about her.
Martin told Anderson at the end of their morning meeting: "I'll never forget this meeting, will you?"
